p.src: Now Yuan Shu, in Huainan, possessed broad lands and abundant grain, as well as the Imperial Seal left with him as surety by Sun Ce; he therefore conceived the ambition of usurping the imperial title. He assembled all his subordinates and said, “In former times, Emperor Gaozu of Han was no more than a village constable on the Si River, yet he won the empire. Now four hundred years have passed, the dynasty’s allotted span is exhausted, and all within the seas is in turmoil. For four generations my family has produced men who held the Three Excellencies, and the people look to us for allegiance. I wish to answer Heaven’s will, follow the people’s desire, and ascend the imperial throne. What do you all think?” Yan Xiang, the chief clerk, said, “You must not. Long ago, Houji of Zhou accumulated virtue and achievement; by the time of King Wen, Zhou possessed two-thirds of the empire, yet still served the Shang. Though your lordship’s lineage is illustrious, its greatness does not equal that of Zhou. And though the House of Han has declined, it has not reached the tyranny of King Zhou of Shang. This course must never be pursued.” Yuan Shu angrily replied, “The Yuan clan descends from Chen. Chen was descended from the great Shun. Earth succeeding Fire accords precisely with the cycle of the elements. Moreover, a prophecy says, ‘He who replaces Han shall be the High One upon the Road.’ My courtesy name is Gonglu—Highway—and it answers the prophecy exactly. I also possess the Imperial Seal of State. If I do not become sovereign, I shall be defying the Way of Heaven. My mind is made up. Whoever says more shall be beheaded!”

p.src: He thereupon founded a dynasty called Zhong, established the offices of the imperial secretariat and other departments, rode in a carriage adorned with dragons and phoenixes, offered sacrifices in the southern and northern suburbs, made Feng Fang’s daughter his empress, and appointed his son crown prince. He then ordered an envoy to press for Lü Bu’s daughter to be brought as the crown prince’s consort. But when he heard that Lü Bu had already sent Han Yin in bonds to the capital at Xu, where Cao Cao had executed him, he flew into a rage. He appointed Zhang Xun General-in-Chief and gave him command of more than two hundred thousand troops, divided into seven armies for the conquest of Xuzhou: the first, under General Zhang Xun, held the center; the second, under Senior General Qiao Rui, took the left; the third, under Senior General Chen Ji, took the right; the fourth, under Deputy General Lei Bo, was on the left; the fifth, under Deputy General Chen Lan, was on the right; the sixth, under the surrendered general Han Xian, was on the left; and the seventh, under the surrendered general Yang Feng, was on the right. Each commander led the valiant officers under him and set out on the appointed day. Yuan Shu appointed Jin Shang, Inspector of Yanzhou, Grand Commandant and charged him with supervising the transport of money and provisions for all seven armies. When Jin Shang refused, Yuan Shu killed him and appointed Ji Ling chief coordinating commander for the seven armies. Yuan Shu himself led thirty thousand troops, appointing Li Feng, Liang Gang, and Yue Jiu as officers to urge the advance and support the seven armies.

p.src: Lü Bu’s scouts learned that Zhang Xun’s army was advancing along the main road directly upon Xuzhou, Qiao Rui’s upon Xiaopei, Chen Ji’s upon Yidu, Lei Bo’s upon Langya, Chen Lan’s upon Jieshi, Han Xian’s upon Xiapi, and Yang Feng’s upon Junshan. The seven armies were marching fifty li a day, pillaging as they came. Lü Bu hurriedly summoned his advisers to deliberate, and Chen Gong and the father and son Chen Gui and Chen Deng all attended. Chen Gong said, “This calamity threatening Xuzhou was brought upon us by Chen Gui and his son. They flattered the court in pursuit of rank and emolument, and today have shifted the disaster onto you, General. Behead them both and offer their heads to Yuan Shu, and his army will withdraw of its own accord.”

p.src: Lü Bu accepted his counsel and at once ordered Chen Gui and Chen Deng seized. Chen Deng laughed loudly and said, “Why are you so fainthearted? To my eyes, the seven armies are no more than seven heaps of rotting straw. Why give them a thought?” Lü Bu said, “If you have a plan to defeat the enemy, I will pardon your capital offense.” Chen Deng replied, “If you will employ this fool’s advice, General, Xuzhou can be kept entirely secure.” Lü Bu said, “Let me hear it.” Chen Deng said, “Though Yuan Shu’s troops are numerous, they are merely a rabble and have never trusted or stood close to one another. If we hold them with regular troops and defeat them with a surprise force, success is certain. I have another plan as well, which will not only preserve Xuzhou but may even take Yuan Shu alive.” Lü Bu asked, “How is this plan to be carried out?” Chen Deng replied, “Han Xian and Yang Feng are former ministers of Han. They fled in fear of Cao Cao and, having nowhere to seek refuge, temporarily submitted to Yuan Shu. Yuan Shu is certain to slight them, and they themselves take no pleasure in serving him. If a brief letter can secure them as allies within, while Liu Bei joins us from without, Yuan Shu will surely be captured.” Lü Bu said, “You must personally go to Han Xian and Yang Feng and deliver the letters.” Chen Deng agreed.

p.src: Lü Bu then sent a memorial to the capital at Xu and a letter to Yuzhou. Afterward he ordered Chen Deng to take a few horsemen and wait for Han Xian on the road to Xiapi. When Han Xian arrived with his army and had finished pitching camp, Chen Deng entered and met him. Han Xian asked, “You are one of Lü Bu’s men. What have you come here for?” Chen Deng smiled and said, “I am an officer of the Great Han. How can you call me one of Lü Bu’s men? As for you, General, you were once a minister of Han, but now you have become the minister of a rebel, reducing to nothing your former merit in protecting the emperor in the passes. I venture to say this is a course unworthy of you. Moreover, Yuan Shu is exceedingly suspicious by nature and will certainly do you harm in the end. If you do not make plans early, regret will come too late.” Han Xian sighed and said, “I wish to return my allegiance to Han, but lament that I have no path by which to do so.” Chen Deng then produced Lü Bu’s letter. After reading it, Han Xian said, “I understand. You should return first. General Yang and I will turn our weapons against Yuan Shu. Watch for flames as our signal; then the Marquis of Wen need only bring his troops to support us.”

p.src: Chen Deng took leave of Han Xian and hurried back to report to Lü Bu. Lü Bu then divided his forces into five armies: Gao Shun led one toward Xiaopei to oppose Qiao Rui. Chen Gong led one toward Yidu to oppose Chen Ji. Zhang Liao and Zang Ba led one out toward Langya to oppose Lei Bo. Song Xian and Wei Xu led one out toward Jieshi to oppose Chen Lan. Lü Bu himself led one along the main road to oppose Zhang Xun. Each commanded ten thousand troops, while the remainder defended the city. Lü Bu marched thirty li from the city and pitched camp. When Zhang Xun’s army arrived, he judged himself no match for Lü Bu. He therefore withdrew twenty li and encamped, awaiting support from the armies on every side.

p.src: That night, during the second watch, Han Xian and Yang Feng divided their forces and set fires throughout the camp, enabling Lü Bu’s troops to break in. Zhang Xun’s army fell into utter confusion. Lü Bu seized the advantage and charged into the slaughter; Zhang Xun fled in defeat. Lü Bu pursued until daybreak, when he ran directly into Ji Ling coming to the rescue. The two armies faced each other and were just about to engage when Han Xian and Yang Feng attacked from two directions. Ji Ling suffered a crushing defeat and fled. Lü Bu led his troops in pursuit, but then another body of soldiers appeared from behind the hills. As the gate banners parted, there appeared a body of troops displaying standards of dragons, phoenixes, sun, and moon, banners of the four measures and five directions, golden maces, silver axes, yellow battle-axes, and white yak-tail standards. Beneath a yellow silk canopy embroidered with gold stood Yuan Shu before the battle line, clad in golden armor with two swords hanging at his wrists. He reviled Lü Bu: “Slave who betrayed his master!”

p.src: Enraged, Lü Bu leveled his halberd and advanced. Yuan Shu’s general Li Feng rode out with leveled spear to meet him. Before three bouts had passed, Lü Bu wounded him in the hand, and Li Feng cast aside his spear and fled. Lü Bu signaled his troops to charge, throwing Yuan Shu’s army into chaos. Lü Bu led his army in pursuit and seized countless horses, garments, and suits of armor. Yuan Shu led his defeated troops away, but before they had gone several li, another body of soldiers emerged from behind a hill and blocked their path. The general at their head was none other than Guan Yunchang. He shouted, “Rebel! Submit to death at once!” Yuan Shu fled in panic, while the rest scattered in every direction; Yunchang fell upon them and slaughtered them fiercely. Yuan Shu gathered his defeated army and fled back to Huainan.

p.src: After his victory, Lü Bu invited Yunchang, Yang Feng, Han Xian, and all their troops to Xuzhou, where he laid out a magnificent banquet in their honor. All the soldiers received rewards. The next day, Yunchang took his leave and returned. Lü Bu recommended Han Xian for appointment as Governor of Yidu. He recommended Yang Feng as Governor of Langya and discussed keeping both men in Xuzhou. Chen Gui said, “You must not. Let Han Xian and Yang Feng occupy the lands east of the mountains. Within a year, every walled city east of the mountains will belong to you, General.” Lü Bu approved. He therefore sent the two generals to station themselves for the time being at Yidu and Langya, there to await the imperial favor and command. Chen Deng privately asked his father, “Why did you not keep the two men in Xuzhou, where they might become the means of killing Lü Bu?” Chen Gui replied, “If the two of them were to assist Lü Bu, we would instead be furnishing the tiger with claws and fangs.” Chen Deng then acknowledged the wisdom of his father’s judgment.

p.src: Now Yuan Shu, having retreated in defeat to Huainan, sent a man to Jiangdong to ask Sun Ce for troops with which to avenge himself. Sun Ce angrily declared, “Relying on my Imperial Seal, you have usurped the imperial title and rebelled against the House of Han—an act of monstrous treason! I am about to send an army to call you to account; how could I instead aid a rebel?” He therefore wrote a letter severing relations with him. The envoy carried the letter back to Yuan Shu. When Yuan Shu had read it, he cried angrily, “How dare that yellow-mouthed brat speak to me so! I shall attack him first!” Only the earnest remonstrance of Chief Clerk Yang Dajiang dissuaded him.

p.src: After sending his letter, Sun Ce guarded against an attack by Yuan Shu, mustering troops to hold the river mouth. Suddenly an envoy arrived from Cao Cao, appointing Sun Ce Administrator of Kuaiji and ordering him to raise troops against Yuan Shu. Sun Ce consulted his advisers and was ready to mobilize at once. Chief Clerk Zhang Zhao said, “Though Yuan Shu has lately been defeated, his troops are numerous and his provisions abundant; we must not underestimate him. We had better write to Cao Cao, urging him to march south, while we support him from the rear. With the two armies supporting each other, Yuan Shu’s army will surely be defeated. And should anything go amiss, we may still look to Cao Cao for rescue.” Sun Ce accepted his counsel and sent an envoy to convey this proposal to Cao Cao.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao reached the capital Xu. Longing for Dian Wei, he established a shrine and offered sacrifices to him; he appointed Dian Wei’s son Dian Man a Gentleman of the Household and took him into his residence to rear him. Suddenly it was reported that Sun Ce had sent an envoy with a letter. After Cao Cao read it, another man reported that Yuan Shu, being short of provisions, was plundering Chenliu; Cao Cao wished to take advantage of his weakness and attack. He therefore raised an army and marched south, ordering Cao Ren to guard the capital Xu while all the others accompanied the expedition: one hundred and seventy thousand cavalry and infantry, with more than a thousand wagons of provisions and baggage. At the same time, he sent men ahead to coordinate with Sun Ce, Liu Bei, and Lü Bu.

Cao Cao exclaimed in surprise, “Whose heads are these?” Xuande replied, “They are the heads of Han Xian and Yang Feng.” “How did you obtain them?” Cao Cao asked. Therefore I arranged a banquet and invited them under the pretense of discussing affairs. During the drinking, I threw down my cup as a signal, whereupon my brothers Guan and Zhang killed them, and I induced all their followers to surrender. p.src: Cao Cao rewarded Xuande handsomely, then joined forces with him and advanced to the borders of Xuzhou. Lü Bu came out to welcome him. Cao Cao soothed him with gracious words, appointed him General of the Left, and promised to exchange his credentials for an official seal and ribbon upon their return to the capital. Lü Bu was overjoyed. Cao Cao then placed Lü Bu’s army on the left and Xuande’s on the right, while he commanded the main army in the center, appointing Xiahou Dun and Yu Jin as vanguards.

p.src: When Yuan Shu learned that Cao Cao’s army was approaching, he ordered his general Qiao Rui to lead fifty thousand troops as the vanguard. The two armies met at the border pass of Shouchun. Qiao Rui rode out first and engaged Xiahou Dun, but before three bouts had passed, Xiahou Dun speared him to death. Yuan Shu’s army was routed and fled back into the city. Suddenly reports came that Sun Ce’s ships were attacking from the west along the river, Lü Bu’s troops from the east, Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei from the south, and Cao Cao himself with one hundred and seventy thousand troops from the north. Yuan Shu was greatly alarmed and hastily assembled all his civil and military officers for counsel. Yang Dajiang said, “Shouchun has suffered successive years of flood and drought, and the people all lack food. Now the mobilization of troops has further afflicted them. Since the people are resentful, it will be difficult to resist when the enemy arrives. It would be better to leave an army in Shouchun and avoid giving battle. When their provisions run out, dissension will surely arise. Your Majesty should meanwhile lead the Imperial Guard across the Huai River. Thus, first, you may go where the harvest is ripe, and second, temporarily avoid the enemy’s keen edge.”

p.src: Now Cao Cao’s one hundred and seventy thousand troops consumed an immense quantity of grain each day, while the commanderies had suffered famine and drought and could not supply enough. p.src: Now Cao Cao led his army back to the capital Xu, where a report came that Duan Wei had killed Li Jue and Wu Xi had killed Guo Si, and that their heads had been brought as offerings. Duan Wei also delivered alive to the capital Xu more than two hundred members of Li Jue’s clan, old and young alike. Cao Cao ordered them divided among the city gates and executed, and their heads displayed as a warning. The people rejoiced. The Emperor ascended the throne hall, assembled the civil and military officials, and held a banquet celebrating the restoration of peace. He appointed Duan Wei General Who Sweeps Away Bandits and Wu Xi General Who Exterminates Rebels, and ordered each to lead troops and guard Chang’an. The two men thanked the Emperor for his favor and departed. Cao Cao then memorialized that Zhang Xiu had rebelled and that an army should be raised to punish him. The Emperor personally ordered out the imperial carriage and escorted Cao Cao as he set forth on campaign. It was the fourth month of summer in the third year of Jian’an.

p.src: Cao Cao left Xun Yu in the capital, Xuchang, to marshal the troops and commanders, while he himself led the main army forth. As the army marched, he saw that the wheat along the road was already ripe. At the army's approach, the people had fled their homes and dared not return to reap the wheat. Cao Cao sent men throughout the surrounding country to proclaim to the village elders and the local officials guarding each district: “I have received His Majesty's explicit decree to lead an army against the rebels and rid the people of this scourge. Though this is the season when the wheat ripens, necessity has compelled me to take the field. Any officer or soldier, high or low, who tramples a wheatfield while passing shall be beheaded. Military law will be enforced with the utmost severity, so let none of you be alarmed or doubtful.” When the people heard the proclamation, all rejoiced and praised him; at the mere sight of the army's dust, they crowded the road and bowed. Whenever the imperial troops crossed a wheatfield, they all dismounted and supported the stalks with their hands, passing them from man to man as they went, and none dared tread upon them.

p.src: As Cao Cao rode onward, a turtledove suddenly flew up in alarm from a field. His horse, startled by the sight, bolted into the wheat and trampled down a large patch. Cao Cao at once summoned the army registrar and ordered him to determine the penalty for his trampling of the wheat. The registrar said, “How could the Chancellor be judged guilty?” Cao Cao said, “I made the law myself, and now I have broken it myself. How then can I command the obedience of the multitude?” He immediately drew his sword and made to cut his own throat. The others hurriedly restrained him. Guo Jia said, “According to the ancient principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals, the law is not applied to those of exalted rank. The Chancellor commands the whole army; how can you take your own life?” Cao Cao pondered for a long while before saying, “Since the Spring and Autumn Annals uphold the principle that the law does not apply to those of exalted rank, I shall for the moment spare myself from death.” He then cut off his own hair with the sword, cast it upon the ground, and said, “For now, let the cutting of my hair stand in place of my head.” He had the hair shown throughout the army with this proclamation: “For trampling the wheat, the Chancellor should by rights have been beheaded as a warning; today his hair has been cut off in its place.” At this, the whole army was struck with awe, and every man observed the military orders with fearful rigor. p.src: Meanwhile, when Zhang Xiu learned that Cao Cao was leading an army against him, he hastily sent a letter to Liu Biao, asking him to provide support from the rear; at the same time, he led his forces out of the city with his two commanders, Lei Xu and Zhang Xian, to meet the enemy. When the two armies had drawn up facing each other, Zhang Xiu rode out, pointed at Cao Cao, and cursed him: “You are a shameless man who makes a pretense of benevolence and righteousness. How are you any different from a beast?” Cao Cao flew into a rage and ordered Xu Chu to ride forth; Zhang Xiu sent Zhang Xian to engage him. In only three bouts, Xu Chu cut down Zhang Xian beneath his horse, and Zhang Xiu's army suffered a crushing defeat. Cao Cao led his army in pursuit as far as the walls of Nanyang. Zhang Xiu entered the city, shut the gates, and refused to come out.

p.src: Cao Cao surrounded the city and attacked, but seeing that its moat was extremely broad and the water deep, making it difficult to approach the walls quickly, he ordered his soldiers to carry earth and fill the moat; he also had sacks of earth mixed with firewood and bundles of grass to construct steps beside the wall; and he erected scaling towers from which to observe the city.
